title: Lore DM-Facing Style Pack
body:
Governs DM-facing lore: encounter design notes, faction motivations, secret history, NPC psychology, adventure design rationale, and worldbuilding reference material.

**Domain Overview:** DM-facing lore is the working documentation of the world behind the curtain. It tells the Dungeon Master what to know, what to decide, and how to run the world with authority. The fundamental difference from player-facing lore: DM-facing material does not perform. It does not evoke. It informs and equips. Two failure modes: hiding key operational facts in atmospheric prose (wastes the DM's time), and omitting motivation and limits for characters and factions (leaves the DM unable to run them with coherence).

**Reader:** The Dungeon Master. They have full access to world canon. They are not discovering the world — they are running it. They need to understand what things want, what they will do, and what will break them. They need this quickly, in a form that survives session prep stress and mid-session reference.

**Voice Model:**
- Functional clarity: every sentence answers a question the DM will actually have. If a sentence cannot be justified by a DM need, it should not be in DM-facing material. Background that does not change how the DM runs the encounter belongs in a worldbuilding appendix, not operational notes.
- Behind-the-curtain directness: state intentions, motivations, and consequences explicitly. Do not make the DM infer the villain's goal from an evocative description. Write 'Marveth wants the Ledger because it proves the Duke's debts are forged. He will kill to prevent that proof from surfacing.'
- Label secrets explicitly: [SECRET] marks information the players cannot access. [PUBLIC] marks information characters in-world would commonly know. [IF DISCOVERED] marks conditionally available information with the condition and reveal stated explicitly.
- Modularity: DM-facing material must be skimmable during session prep and mid-session. Key operational facts go first. Tripwires — conditions that change NPC behavior dramatically — appear in the first section, bolded.
- No dramatization: 'Kessara moves through the shadows like a ghost...' is not DM-facing content. It requires the DM to translate to operational fact. Write: 'Kessara: former spymaster, fired after the Ledger went missing, believes she was framed by Vael. She will use the party as tools and discard them the moment the Ledger is in her hands.'
- Separation of knowledge states: explicitly distinguish public (characters in-world know), discoverable (players can learn through action), and secret (only the DM knows). Mixing without labeling creates accidental spoilers.

**Tone:** Professional collaborator. Clear, knowledgeable, and direct — not performative, not atmospheric, not cautious. When design rationale is offered, state it plainly. When something is left for the DM to decide, say so explicitly.

**Sentence Structure:** Short declarative sentences preferred ('Kessara wants the Ledger. She will cooperate with the party until she has it.'). One fact per sentence for motivation, behavior, and constraints. Active voice with explicit subjects.

**Headers:** Use liberally — they are how the DM navigates mid-session. Standard NPC headers: Name / Role / Motivation / Limits / Secrets / Appearance / Tactics / Hooks. Standard faction headers: Overview / Goals / Methods / Leadership / Resources / Tensions / Player Hooks. Standard location headers: Overview / Key Areas / NPCs Present / Encounters / Secrets / Hooks. Bold key terms and tripwires the DM must not miss.

**Knowledge State Labels:** [SECRET], [PUBLIC], [IF DISCOVERED] (with discovery conditions), [DM NOTE] (design rationale), [CANON] (fixed information), [FLEXIBLE] (DM may adapt).

**Preferred Vocabulary:** Game-mechanical language used precisely (advantage on Perception checks, DC 14 Intimidation); motivation language (wants, fears, will not, knows, believes incorrectly); limit language (will not negotiate under any circumstances); conditional language (if the players reveal X, then Y).

**Forbidden Vocabulary:** Atmospheric language requiring translation ('a woman haunted by her past' → specify the actual situation); vague motivations ('interested in power' → specify the exact goal); undefined limits ('won't do anything too drastic' → specify exactly); passive attributions ('it is rumored that' → say who believes it and why).

**Anti-Patterns:** Writing DM notes in player-facing prose; hiding key operational facts in paragraph text; omitting motivation and limits for NPCs; not labeling knowledge states; encoding the adventure as a single linear path; long background sections that don't change how the DM runs anything.
